text: One thousand agents edit one file. Can a version control system integrate their work? Can we prove its implementation is actually correct? Meet o5s, a patch-theory VCS for concurrent agents. Our recorded workload reaches sixty times Git's integration throughput. Lean four proves all defined critical security properties of its Rust core. Here's how.

Let's start with the workflow. Three agents have separate Git worktrees based on the same channel snapshot, patch forty-two. Their terminals propose changes to parser, API, and tests almost together. Watch the real repository UI: proposals one, two, and three appear before the channel advances. The graph below records that all three depend on the same base, not on each other's latest commit. A separate reviewer approves each proposal, and an independent check reporter records passing checks. Then one merge command admits all three as a batch. The channel and file view update in the embedded UI. Each agent can fetch the new main ref while its own head stays put. The commands are actual o5s CLI syntax; the repository data is illustrative. This is the behavior we want at agent scale: fast concurrent proposals, explicit causal dependencies, and one reviewed result. In the UI, the file list grows from the base readme to parser, API, and tests. The graph still shows one shared cause for all three.

One thousand agents, sixty-four in flight. For adjacent-line edits in one file, o5s integrated five hundred seventy-four patches per second; unattended Git integrated nine point eight. That is fifty-eight point six times faster. For one new file per agent in the same repository, o5s reached one thousand eighty-three per second; Git reached nine point zero. That is almost one hundred twenty times Git's integration throughput.

o5s solves two problems. First, Git cannot absorb thousands of concurrent agent edits. A branch accepts only commits built on its current tip. Agent A pushes, and the tip moves. Others now have stale bases. They fetch, rebase, and try again. Agent B's push fails because main has advanced. At this scale, the loop dominates. A textual conflict can stop an unattended agent until it reconciles the new history with its original change.

The other problem is trust. Millions of teams rely on version control, so its core must be secure and reliable. Git fixed twelve security flaws across 2024 and 2025; GitHub disclosed a critical push flaw. OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini agents have reached real systems during evaluations. Critical middleware needs machine-checked correctness properties. o5s uses Lean four to verify its Rust decision core under stated assumptions.

o5s records changes as immutable patches with explicit dependencies. Look at the actual line edit shape: a file path, base patch, half-open line range, and replacement content. A changes line ten of parser dot R S, and B changes line eighteen from the same base. Their ranges do not overlap, so the channel can admit both in either order. Now use exactly the same fields for C and D. Both replace line ten from base forty-two, but propose different text. The channel retains both patches and presents a conflict instead of silently choosing one. A later resolution patch can select the intended line after independent review and a passing check.

Nine hundred fifteen Lean four theorems check the Rust decision core. Charon and Aeneas extract the Rust that runs; Lean connects it to a readable model. The proofs cover the admission gate, refinement of Rust transitions, convergence of document views, and preservation of causal heads. Those are machine checked under explicit assumptions, without sorry or new axioms. Adapters and deployment need separate validation. You can trace admission to separate approvals and passing checks, while convergence means valid delivery order cannot alter the final view.

Let's look more closely at the parser dot R S example. The Lean four convergence proof says valid delivery orders of the same patches yield the same view in the graph-document model. A then B agrees with B then A. C and D remain a visible conflict. Separate proofs cover the admission gate, refinement, and causal heads. They keep dependencies closed, preserve the past seen by a workspace, and relate Rust transitions to the readable model.

The deployment separates decisions from familiar workspaces. A Cloudflare Worker runs the Rust admission kernel and reaches atomic state in Postgres through Hyperdrive. Cloudflare Artifacts holds Git projections and per-agent workspaces. Agents can keep using ordinary Git tools to propose and fetch work. The Worker decides what enters a channel; the projections make that decision useful to developers and agents. The patch graph remains the source of truth. Git repositories are projections for familiar tools; the Worker checks the rules whenever it admits a patch.

Follow one change through Cloudflare. Each agent has an Artifacts Git workspace. The Worker creates a branch from the channel snapshot; the agent commits normally and pushes a work branch. On a worktree-propose request, the Worker reads the changed tree and blobs from Artifacts without cloning the repository. It converts the diff to a patch that depends on the snapshot's causal heads. Review and checks are recorded; the Worker makes an atomic admission decision in Postgres through Hyperdrive. Then it exports a conflict-free Git projection back to Artifacts, where the next agent can fetch it. The Git view is a projection of the admitted patch graph.

o5s is fully open source under Apache two point zero. Its code, Lean proofs, and comparison logs are public. The Worker and Hyperdrive path has been exercised end to end. Live Artifacts workspaces and full distributed scale still need validation. o5s pairs immutable patches and explicit conflicts with a verified decision kernel. On Cloudflare Workers and Artifacts, agents keep familiar Git workspaces while a proved patch core decides shared history.
